In the general population, having disease A and having disease B are completely statistically independent. A certain hospital admits only patients who have at least one of the two diseases (A, B, or both). Among only the patients admitted to this hospital, researchers find that having disease A makes it LESS likely a patient also has disease B, even though the diseases are independent in the general population. What explains this?
choices: Berkson's paradox: conditioning on being admitted (having A or B) induces a spurious negative correlation between the independent causes of admission
This is impossible — truly independent traits cannot appear correlated in any subgroup
Disease A must be biologically protective against disease B
The hospital's sample size is too small to draw any real conclusion

questions.q: A basketball player has an independent 75% chance of making any given free throw, unaffected by prior makes or misses, and has just made 9 in a row. Commentators say he's 'heating up' and is now more likely than usual to make the next one. What is the actual probability he makes his 10th free throw?
choices: Lower than 75%, because streaks must break
It depends on how many more shots remain in the game
Higher than 75%, because he's in the zone

questions.q: In a single round of the Ultimatum Game, Player A is given $100 and proposes how to split it with Player B. Player B can only accept (both keep their share) or reject (both get nothing) — there are no further rounds. Assuming both players are purely rational and self-interested, caring only about maximizing their own money, and the split can be made in $1 increments, what split should Player A propose?
choices: A 50/50 split, since it's the fairest outcome
It cannot be determined without knowing Player B's personal values
Keep all $100 and give Player B nothing
Give Player B $1 and keep $99, the smallest offer B should still accept

questions.q: You have two glasses holding exactly equal volumes of liquid — one full of wine, one full of water. You take a spoonful of wine from the wine glass and stir it into the water glass. Then, without measuring, you take a spoonful of the now-mixed liquid from the water glass and stir it back into the wine glass, so both glasses once again hold equal volumes. Is there now more water in the wine glass, or more wine in the water glass?
choices: More wine in the water glass than water in the wine glass
Exactly the same amount either way, regardless of how thoroughly it was mixed
More water in the wine glass than wine in the water glass
It cannot be determined without knowing the size of the spoon

questions.q: Three voters rank three candidates A, B, and C as follows — Voter 1: A > B > C. Voter 2: B > C > A. Voter 3: C > A > B. In pairwise majority votes, A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A, each by 2 votes to 1 — so the group's collective preference cycles even though every individual voter's own ranking is perfectly transitive. What is this phenomenon called?

questions.q: Which is larger: the number of distinct ways to shuffle a standard 52-card deck (52!), or the number of atoms on Earth (roughly 10^50)?
choices: It's impossible to meaningfully compare a permutation count to a physical count
The number of atoms on Earth — a mere 52 cards can't compete with atoms
The number of ways to shuffle a deck of cards (52!) — it vastly exceeds the number of atoms on Earth
They are roughly equal, both around 10^50
